newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Steelmaker's collapse shakes S.Korean banks.
newsitem.headline: Steelmaker's collapse shakes S.Korean banks.

text.p: The collapse of a second South Korean steelmaker this year has highlighted a mountain of bad debt amassed by domestic banks after decades of reckless lending, analysts said on Thursday.
While financial authorities sought to allay fears of a banking sector crisis following the latest corporate casualty, foreign lenders showed further signs of cold feet.
"Foreign banks that said they would offer us loans last week suddenly turned their backs on us today," said a loans manager at a leading domestic bank.
Sammi Steel Co sought court protection on Tuesday in a further shock to a banking system reeling from the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co in January in South Korea's biggest bankruptcy.
European rating agency IBCA on Wednesday downgraded the individual ratings of Korea First Bank, Cho Hung Bank and Korea Exchange Bank.
Moody's Investors Service dropped the long-term ratings of those banks last month.
South Korean banks funded the nation's rise to economic "tiger" status from the ashes of World War Two, extending loans to politically-favoured companies in their role as virtual government cashiers.
Grand projects and big industrial conglomerates were given priority over small and medium-sized companies. Credit analysis counted for little, analysts said.
"Over 90 percent of bad debt at local banks are policy loans," said Kim Chul-jung, a banking analyst at Ssangyong Investment Securities.

Kim said 4.5 percent of all outstanding loans of eight major banks were non-performing at the end of last year. But following the Hanbo and Sammi crisis, he estimated the ratio had jumped to 7.4 percent.
Bank of Korea figures show only 0.8 percent of all bank loans are non-performing, but based on a narrow definition.
"What banks really need to improve is management independence from the government," said Kim Sung-soo, a banking analyst at Hyundai Securities.
Sammi's woes are expected to trigger a further rise in the "Korea Premium", or the extra cost of money imposed on Korean banks in international markets.
Domestic banks have been paying more for their loans since the collapse of Hanbo.
They are paying 45-50 basis points above London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) for one to six month term deposits. Before the Hanbo collapse they were being offered 25-30 basis points above LIBOR.
Banks exposed to Sammi Steel hurried to report their positions, fearing further damage to their reputations.

Korea First Bank said it had 217.4 billion won ($245 million) of outstanding loans to Sammi Steel, the largest of any financial institution, while state-run Korea Development Bank put its exposure at 16.4 billion.
A central bank official said Korea First was not in trouble, and he denied media reports that the Bank of Korea was planning to extend emergency loans to the bank.
"Korea First Bank has no funding problem at all despite Sammi," said Park Chul, director of the central bank's monetary policy division.
Banks also have been hammered by stock market losses.
Plunging share prices wiped 4.96 trillion won from the investment portfolios of the country's 25 commercial banks last year, according to central bank statistics. (Conversion: $1 = 884 won)
